notes: \cpara{Opens with two defenses of reverence for the Bible on new grounds, as a guide to ethics and as literature. The Harris quotation is exact; the exchange with Andrew Sullivan is now at samharris.org under the title ``Is Religion Built Upon Lies?'', since the footnote's address no longer works. The opening claim, that ``Many Christians who've stopped really believing'' hold this view, is a claim about what those Christians believe, and no example or evidence is given for it.}

\cpara{The second example, a hypothetical one: a friend defends a \$1 million laptop by its effect on the economy, and the post answers with a better way to serve the same goal, 5,000 One Laptop Per Child machines.}

\cpara{Refers back, without naming them, to ``The Third Alternative'' (May 2007) and ``Motivated Stopping and Motivated Continuation'' (four days earlier), and separates the laptop case from motivated stopping: here no search took place at all.}

\cpara{States the post's test, drawn from ``The Bottom Line'': a justification counts only if it is a new search that could change the conclusion. The recap matches that post's claim that effectiveness is set by ``whichever algorithm actually writes the bottom line.'' A justification of this kind is what the dictionary calls rationalizing; see the notes on ``Rationalization.''}
\clogic{A claim about most criticism, given with no evidence.}
\cpara{Says what a real justification of the Bible's literary standing would take: a neutral reading of candidate books, with renown as a fair way to choose the candidates.}

\clogic{The neutrality requirement is applied to one side only. The post's own verdicts in its first paragraph, that \textsc{The Lord of the Rings} is ``a vastly superior literary work'' and that even \textsc{Harry Potter} is superior ``as moral philosophy,'' come with no reading shown. A reader who has already rejected the Bible also has a bottom line, and the post does not ask where it came from.}

\cpara{Asserts that ``No search ever occurred'' for these believers, and gives no case. What the setup establishes is that the reverence came first. The next paragraph grants that a later check does count if it could change the conclusion, so whether one took place is a question of fact about each person.}
\cpara{Grants that a real check changes ``the real algorithm'' behind a conclusion, then says people greatly overestimate their readiness to change their minds.}

\clogic{No evidence is given here, but the author had given evidence four weeks earlier, in ``We Change Our Minds Less Often Than We Think'' (3 October 2007). There the author quotes Griffin and Tversky: colleagues choosing between job offers gave the option they expected to choose an average probability of 66\%, and 23 of the 24 chose it. It is one small study, and it points the way this sentence says.}
\cpara{A one-line joke on the same point.}
\cpara{Returns to the laptop buyer, now imagined as having adopted an altruistic goal afterwards and found that the original purchase still comes out best under it.}

\cpara{The post's central argument, and it is sound as stated. When the process that produced a choice has nothing to do with the criterion now used to defend it, it would be a coincidence for the choice to be the criterion's best answer. The laptop case also shows how to test for it: look for an option that does better under the new criterion.}
\cpara{Closes with a maxim, hedged with ``improbable,'' which the previous paragraph supports.}
